page: What are the advantages and disadvantages of HRRN scheduling?

text: CPU Scheduling — Analogies, Comparisons and Common Doubts.
title: Introduction
page: Introduction

text: Think of a single billing counter at a canteen. Whoever joins the line first is served first, and the cashier never stops serving one customer to serve another. That is First Come First Served: the ready queue is a FIFO queue, the process at the head gets the CPU, and it keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or requests I/O. It is simple and fair in the sense that nobody jumps the queue, but if the first customer has a huge order, everyone behind them waits. That waiting is the convoy effect, and it is why FCFS usually has a poor average waiting time.
title: Explain FCFS scheduling with an analogy
page: Explain FCFS scheduling with an analogy

text: Think of a single counter serving five customers, where the clerk spends at most two minutes with each person before moving to the next one in line. If your work is not finished, you go to the back of the line and wait for your next turn. Round Robin works the same way: the ready queue is circular, each process gets one time quantum, and when the timer expires the process is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue. Nobody waits forever, so there is no starvation, and short jobs finish quickly, which gives good response time. The price is more context switches.
title: Explain Round Robin scheduling with an analogy
page: Explain Round Robin scheduling with an analogy

text: Imagine a photocopy shop where the operator always picks the customer with the fewest pages next. Customers with one page are done almost instantly, so the average time people spend waiting is as low as it can be. That is SJF: among the ready processes, the one with the smallest next CPU burst runs first, with FCFS breaking ties. It is provably optimal for average waiting time. Its weaknesses are that the scheduler must predict burst lengths and that a customer with a hundred pages may keep getting pushed back, which is starvation.
title: Explain Shortest Job First scheduling with an analogy
page: Explain Shortest Job First scheduling with an analogy

text: In priority scheduling every process carries a priority number and the CPU always goes to the ready process with the highest priority. In our course a lower number means a higher priority, so a process with priority 1 runs before one with priority 3. Processes with equal priority are served in FCFS order. It can be non-preemptive, where a newly arrived high-priority process waits for the current burst to finish, or preemptive, where it takes the CPU immediately. The main risk is starvation of low-priority processes, which is solved by aging.
title: Explain Priority scheduling
page: Explain Priority scheduling

text: The convoy effect happens under FCFS when one long CPU-bound process holds the CPU and many short processes queue up behind it, like cars stuck behind a slow truck on a single-lane road. The short processes could have finished quickly, but they all wait for the long one. Meanwhile I/O devices sit idle because the I/O-bound processes are stuck in the ready queue. The result is a high average waiting time and lower CPU and device utilisation. Algorithms that pick the shortest job first, such as SJF, reduce it because short processes are not stuck behind a long one; Round Robin limits it by preempting a long process after one quantum, but it does not choose short jobs first.
title: What is the convoy effect?
page: What is the convoy effect?

text: Starvation, also called indefinite blocking, is when a ready process waits for the CPU indefinitely because the scheduler keeps choosing other processes. It happens in SJF and SRTF when short jobs keep arriving and a long job is always passed over, and in priority scheduling when higher-priority processes keep arriving and a low-priority process never gets its turn. Under standard assumptions (every process that runs eventually finishes or blocks, and the ready queue is finite ahead of a waiting process), FCFS and Round Robin do not cause starvation because every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. Waiting a long time behind a long job in FCFS is the convoy effect, which is a delay and not starvation. The standard remedy is aging.
title: What is starvation in CPU scheduling?
page: What is starvation in CPU scheduling?

text: Aging is a technique that gradually raises the priority of a process the longer it waits in the ready queue. For example, the scheduler might improve a waiting process's priority by 1 every 15 minutes. Eventually even the lowest-priority process becomes the highest-priority one and gets the CPU. It is needed because plain priority scheduling, and SJF which is a special case of it, can starve low-priority or long processes forever. Aging guarantees that every process makes progress.
title: What is aging and why is it needed?
page: What is aging and why is it needed?

text: Turnaround time is the total time from when a process arrives to when it completes: turnaround = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time is the total time the process spends sitting in the ready queue: waiting = turnaround time − burst time. Response time is the time from arrival until the process gets the CPU for the first time: response = first start time − arrival time. For non-preemptive algorithms response time equals waiting time, because once a process starts it runs to completion.
title: Define waiting time, turnaround time and response time
page: Define waiting time, turnaround time and response time

text: In non-preemptive (cooperative) scheduling, once a process gets the CPU it keeps it until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. In preemptive scheduling the operating system can take the CPU away from a running process, for example when a timer interrupt fires or when a more important process arrives. Examples of non-preemptive algorithms are FCFS and SJF; examples of preemptive ones are Round Robin and SRTF; Priority scheduling can be either. Preemption improves response time but adds context-switch overhead.
title: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
page: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?

text: A context switch is the act of saving the state of the currently running process and loading the saved state of the next process to run. The state, including the program counter, registers and memory-management information, is stored in the process control block (PCB). Context switches happen whenever the scheduler moves the CPU from one process to another, for example when a Round Robin quantum expires. They are pure overhead: no user work is done during the switch, so systems try to keep them infrequent.
title: What is a context switch?
page: What is a context switch?

text: The dispatcher is the module that actually gives control of the CPU to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler. Its job has three parts: switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the user program to resume it. Because it runs on every process switch, it should be as fast as possible. The time it takes to stop one process and start another is called the dispatch latency.
title: What is the role of the dispatcher?
page: What is the role of the dispatcher?

text: Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.
title: Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling
page: Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling

text: Since the scheduler cannot know the future, it predicts the next burst as an exponential average of the past ones: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n). Here t(n) is the actual length of the most recent burst, τ(n) is the previous prediction, and α is between 0 and 1, commonly 1/2. With α = 0 the prediction never changes; with α = 1 only the last burst matters. With α = 1/2, recent and past history count equally.
title: How is the length of the next CPU burst predicted in SJF?
page: How is the length of the next CPU burst predicted in SJF?

text: The quantum decides how Round Robin behaves. If the quantum is very large, longer than every burst, no process is ever preempted and Round Robin becomes FCFS. If the quantum is very small, the CPU spends a large share of its time context switching instead of running processes. The quantum should therefore be large compared with the context-switch time; a common rule of thumb is that about 80 percent of CPU bursts should be shorter than the quantum.
title: How does the size of the time quantum affect Round Robin?
page: How does the size of the time quantum affect Round Robin?

text: Round Robin preempts the running process every time its quantum expires, even if it has only a little work left. Each preemption is a context switch: the CPU state is saved into the PCB, the next process's state is loaded, and caches and the TLB may be disturbed. A process with burst 10 and quantum 1 causes 9 switches by itself, while FCFS or SJF would cause none during that burst. So the smaller the quantum, the more of the CPU's time is lost to switching.
title: Why does Round Robin have higher context-switch overhead?
page: Why does Round Robin have higher context-switch overhead?

text: SJF is optimal because moving a short job ahead of a long job reduces the short job's waiting time by the long job's burst, but increases the long job's waiting time only by the short job's burst. Since the short burst is smaller, the total waiting time goes down every time we make such a swap. Keep swapping until the jobs are sorted by burst length and you reach the arrangement with the minimum total, and therefore minimum average, waiting time.
title: Why is SJF optimal for average waiting time?
page: Why is SJF optimal for average waiting time?

text: Scheduling algorithms are compared on five criteria. CPU utilisation, keeping the CPU as busy as possible, and throughput, the number of processes completed per unit time, should be maximised. Turnaround time, the time from arrival to completion; waiting time, the time spent in the ready queue; and response time, the time until the first response, should be minimised. In exam numericals the usual comparison is the average waiting time and average turnaround time.
title: What are the CPU scheduling criteria?
page: What are the CPU scheduling criteria?

text: A multilevel feedback queue has several ready queues with different priorities, and it lets processes move between them. A process that uses its whole quantum, behaving like a CPU-bound job, is moved down to a lower-priority queue. A process that waits too long in a lower queue is moved up, which is a form of aging. Interactive, I/O-bound processes therefore stay in the high-priority queues and get good response time, and no process starves.
title: What is a multilevel feedback queue?
page: What is a multilevel feedback queue?

text: Scheduling decisions can happen at four moments: when a process switches from running to waiting, for example on an I/O request; from running to ready, for example on a timer interrupt; from waiting to ready, when its I/O completes; and when a process terminates. If the scheduler only acts in the first and last cases, the scheme is non-preemptive. If it can also act in the other two, it is preemptive.
title: When do CPU scheduling decisions take place?
page: When do CPU scheduling decisions take place?

text: A context switch typically takes on the order of microseconds, so a quantum of 10 to 100 milliseconds keeps switching overhead to a tiny fraction of CPU time while still giving interactive users a turn many times per second. Much smaller and the CPU would spend too much time switching; much larger and Round Robin would behave like FCFS and interactive response would suffer.
title: Why is a time quantum of 10 to 100 milliseconds used in practice?
page: Why is a time quantum of 10 to 100 milliseconds used in practice?

text: Yes. SJF is priority scheduling where the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst: the shorter the predicted burst, the higher the priority. That is why SJF shares priority scheduling's main weakness, starvation of the processes with the lowest priority, which in SJF are the long jobs.
title: Is SJF a special case of priority scheduling?
page: Is SJF a special case of priority scheduling?

text: Step 1: list every process with its arrival time, burst time and, if needed, priority. Step 2: simulate the algorithm on a time line, deciding at every scheduling point which ready process runs. Step 3: draw the Gantt chart, including idle gaps when no process has arrived. Step 4: read each completion time off the chart. Step 5: compute turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst. Step 6: average each column. Most lost marks come from a wrong tie-break or a wrongly ordered Round Robin queue.

page: Explain how to solve a CPU scheduling numerical step by step

text: SJF deliberately favours short processes: it picks the shortest burst first, so short processes run almost immediately and the average waiting time is the minimum possible, but long jobs can starve. Round Robin does not prioritise short processes: it gives every process one quantum in cyclic order. A short process that fits in one quantum finishes in its first turn, but it may have to wait a turn for each process ahead of it. SJF wins on average waiting time; Round Robin wins on fairness and response time, and under standard assumptions no process starves.
title: Compare SJF and Round Robin for short processes
page: Compare SJF and Round Robin for short processes

text: FCFS is non-preemptive: each process runs to completion in arrival order, so it has very few context switches but suffers from the convoy effect and poor response time. Round Robin is FCFS plus a timer: each process runs for at most one quantum and then goes to the back of the queue. That gives good response time and fairness for interactive users at the cost of more context switches. If the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS.
title: Compare FCFS and Round Robin
page: Compare FCFS and Round Robin

text: Both choose the process with the least CPU work, but SJF is non-preemptive and SRTF is preemptive. In SJF, once a process starts it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. In SRTF, a newly arrived process with a burst shorter than the running process's remaining time preempts it. On the textbook example with bursts 8, 4, 9, 5 arriving at 0, 1, 2, 3, SJF gives an average waiting time of 7.75 and SRTF gives 6.50. SRTF is better on waiting time but needs more context switches.
title: Compare SJF and SRTF
page: Compare SJF and SRTF

text: FCFS serves processes in arrival order and SJF serves the shortest burst first. On P1 = 6, P2 = 8, P3 = 7, P4 = 3 all arriving at 0, FCFS gives an average waiting time of 10.25 while SJF gives 7.00. SJF is optimal for average waiting time, but it needs burst lengths to be known or predicted and it can starve long jobs. FCFS needs no prediction and never starves anyone, but it suffers from the convoy effect.
title: Compare FCFS and SJF
page: Compare FCFS and SJF

text: Both always run the highest-priority ready process. The difference is what happens when a higher-priority process arrives while another is running. In the non-preemptive version, the newcomer is placed at the head of the ready queue and waits until the current burst finishes. In the preemptive version, the running process is interrupted immediately and the newcomer takes the CPU. The preemptive version responds faster to important work but causes more context switches; both can starve low-priority processes without aging.
title: Compare preemptive and non-preemptive priority scheduling
page: Compare preemptive and non-preemptive priority scheduling

text: Round Robin is the algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Every user's process gets the CPU for one quantum at regular intervals, so each user sees a responsive system and, under standard assumptions, no ready process is starved. FCFS is a poor choice because one long job can hold everyone up, and SJF needs burst prediction and can starve long jobs. Real systems often use a multilevel feedback queue, which uses Round Robin within each level.
title: Which scheduling algorithm is best for time-sharing systems?
page: Which scheduling algorithm is best for time-sharing systems?

text: Standard FCFS does not cause starvation, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue provided the processes ahead of it terminate. Standard Round Robin does not cause starvation either: with n ready processes and a finite quantum q, every ready process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. SJF and SRTF can starve long jobs if short ones keep arriving. Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving. For the last two, aging is the standard fix.
title: Compare the algorithms on starvation
page: Compare the algorithms on starvation

text: FCFS and non-preemptive SJF switch only when a process finishes or blocks, so they have the lowest overhead. Non-preemptive priority is the same. SRTF and preemptive priority add a switch every time a better process arrives. Round Robin has the highest overhead because it switches at every quantum expiry, and the smaller the quantum, the more switches.
title: Compare the algorithms on context-switch overhead
page: Compare the algorithms on context-switch overhead

text: Round Robin interleaves all processes, so a process that could have finished early keeps being paused while others take their turns, which pushes completion times later. SJF lets the shortest job finish completely before starting the next, which minimises the average completion and turnaround time. Round Robin trades turnaround time for response time: every process starts quickly even though most finish later.
title: Why does Round Robin have higher average turnaround time than SJF?
page: Why does Round Robin have higher average turnaround time than SJF?

text: Under FCFS a process's response time equals its waiting time, because it starts only after every earlier process has finished; a short process stuck behind a long one may wait a very long time to start. Under Round Robin every process gets its first turn within (n − 1) × q time units, so response time is short and predictable. That is why Round Robin suits interactive systems and FCFS suits batch systems.
title: Compare response time under FCFS and Round Robin
page: Compare response time under FCFS and Round Robin

text: SJF is a special case of priority scheduling where the priority is the inverse of the next CPU burst. General priority scheduling lets the priority come from anything, such as importance, memory needs or user type. Both can be preemptive or non-preemptive, both pick the best ready process at every decision point, and both can starve the processes they rank lowest, which aging solves.
title: Compare SJF and Priority scheduling
page: Compare SJF and Priority scheduling

text: FCFS is a reasonable choice for batch systems where jobs are not interactive and minimising overhead matters more than response time. It needs no timer and causes the fewest context switches. Round Robin is the better choice when users are waiting at a terminal and need regular turns. If the bursts are all short compared with the quantum, the two behave almost identically.
title: When would you choose FCFS over Round Robin?
page: When would you choose FCFS over Round Robin?

text: No, that is a common mix-up. Round Robin does not cause starvation: the ready queue is circular, so every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, where n is the number of processes and q is the quantum. What Round Robin does cause is extra context-switch overhead and a higher average turnaround time than SJF. Starvation is a problem of SJF, SRTF and priority scheduling, where a process can be passed over again and again.
title: A student says Round Robin causes starvation. Is this correct?
page: A student says Round Robin causes starvation. Is this correct?

text: No. If short jobs keep arriving, there is always a job shorter than the long one, so the long job can be passed over indefinitely. Nothing in SJF guarantees that the long job ever becomes the shortest. That is exactly starvation. Aging, which raises a job's priority the longer it waits, is the standard fix.
title: A student says SJF never causes starvation because every job is eventually the shortest. Is this right?
page: A student says SJF never causes starvation because every job is eventually the shortest. Is this right?

text: No, that formula gives the turnaround time. Turnaround = completion − arrival is the total time the process spends in the system. Waiting time removes the time spent actually running: waiting = turnaround − burst. For example, a process that arrives at 0, has burst 3 and completes at 27 has turnaround 27 but waiting time 24.
title: A student says waiting time equals completion time minus arrival time. Is that correct?
page: A student says waiting time equals completion time minus arrival time. Is that correct?

text: Not always. A larger quantum reduces context-switch overhead, but once the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin becomes FCFS and inherits the convoy effect and poor response time. A very small quantum, on the other hand, wastes time on switching. The best quantum sits in between: large compared with the context-switch time, with about 80 percent of bursts shorter than it.
title: A student says a larger Round Robin quantum always gives better performance. Is this true?
page: A student says a larger Round Robin quantum always gives better performance. Is this true?

text: It depends on the convention, and in our course it is the other way round. Following the prescribed textbook, a lower number means a higher priority, so priority 1 runs before priority 3. Always check the convention stated in the question; if none is given, use the textbook's. Getting this backwards reverses the whole Gantt chart.
title: A student says in priority scheduling a higher number means higher priority. Is this correct?
page: A student says in priority scheduling a higher number means higher priority. Is this correct?

text: No. When a process arrives at the same instant that the running process's quantum expires, the new arrival is added to the ready queue first and the preempted process is placed behind it. Putting them in the wrong order is the most common error in Round Robin numericals, and it changes every waiting time after that point.
title: A student says in Round Robin the preempted process goes back to the queue before a process that arrives at the same moment. Is this correct?
page: A student says in Round Robin the preempted process goes back to the queue before a process that arrives at the same moment. Is this correct?

text: Not always. FCFS is generally poor, but its result depends on arrival order. If the processes happen to arrive shortest first, FCFS produces exactly the SJF order and the optimal average waiting time. For P2 = 3, P3 = 3, P1 = 24 arriving in that order, FCFS gives an average of 3.00, but in the order P1, P2, P3 it gives 17.00.
title: A student says FCFS is always the worst algorithm for average waiting time. Is that right?
page: A student says FCFS is always the worst algorithm for average waiting time. Is that right?

text: No, that describes non-preemptive SJF. SRTF is the preemptive version: whenever a new process arrives with a burst shorter than the remaining time of the running process, the running process is preempted. In the textbook example, P1 starts at 0 with burst 8, and at time 1 P2 arrives with burst 4, which is less than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is preempted.
title: A student says SRTF never preempts a process once it has started. Is this right?
page: A student says SRTF never preempts a process once it has started. Is this right?

text: Only for non-preemptive algorithms. In FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive priority, a process runs to completion once started, so the time until it first runs is all the waiting it ever does. In Round Robin or SRTF a process can be preempted and wait again later, so its total waiting time can be much larger than its response time.
title: A student says response time and waiting time are always equal. Is this correct?
page: A student says response time and waiting time are always equal. Is this correct?

text: No. During a context switch the CPU saves the old process's state into its PCB and loads the new one's, and caches and the TLB may need to be refilled afterwards. No user work is done during this time, so it is pure overhead. With a very small Round Robin quantum this overhead can take a large share of CPU time.
title: A student says context switching is free because the CPU is fast. Is this true?
page: A student says context switching is free because the CPU is fast. Is this true?

text: No. Waiting time only counts time a process spends in the ready queue after it has arrived. If the CPU is idle because no process has arrived yet, that idle gap belongs to no process. You still draw the idle gap on the Gantt chart, but each process's waiting time is turnaround − burst, where turnaround starts at that process's own arrival time.
title: A student says the idle time at the start of a Gantt chart counts as waiting time. Is that right?
page: A student says the idle time at the start of a Gantt chart counts as waiting time. Is that right?

text: No, it becomes FCFS, not SJF. With a quantum larger than every burst, no process is ever preempted, so processes simply run to completion in queue order, which is arrival order. SJF would instead reorder them by burst length.
title: A student says Round Robin with a very large quantum is the same as SJF. Is this correct?
page: A student says Round Robin with a very large quantum is the same as SJF. Is this correct?

text: No, it's the opposite: Round Robin has more context switches than FCFS or SJF, not fewer. It preempts the running process every time its time quantum expires, even if the process still has work left, and each preemption is a context switch. A process with burst 10 and quantum 1 alone causes 9 switches; FCFS or non-preemptive SJF running that same process would cause none. The smaller the quantum, the more switching overhead Round Robin pays.
title: A friend says Round Robin has no context switches. Is this right?
page: A friend says Round Robin has no context switches. Is this right?

text: CPU Scheduling — Commonly Confused Concepts (convoy effect, starvation, aging, who favours short jobs). Standard assumptions used in this note: every process that gets the CPU eventually finishes or blocks for I/O, the number of processes ahead of a waiting process is finite, and Round Robin uses a finite time quantum.
title: Introduction
page: Introduction

text: The convoy effect is a performance problem: a long CPU-bound process holds the CPU and many short processes wait behind it, so average waiting time rises and CPU and I/O-device utilisation fall. It is classically associated with FCFS, which is non-preemptive and serves processes in arrival order. Every waiting process still gets the CPU eventually, so the delay is long but finite. Starvation (indefinite blocking or indefinite postponement) is different: a ready process is passed over again and again and may never get the CPU. It can happen in SJF and SRTF when shorter jobs keep arriving ahead of a long job, and in Priority scheduling when higher-priority processes keep arriving ahead of a low-priority one. Under the standard assumptions, FCFS does not cause starvation and Round Robin does not either, because every ready process gets a turn within (n − 1) × q time units. Aging, which gradually raises the priority of a waiting process, is the usual remedy for starvation in priority-based scheduling. In short: the convoy effect is a long wait that ends, caused by a long job at the front; starvation is a wait that may never end, caused by the scheduler's selection rule.
title: What is the difference between the convoy effect and starvation?
page: What is the difference between the convoy effect and starvation?

text: Convoy effect example under FCFS: P1 needs 100 time units and arrives first, then P2 and P3 need 2 units each. P2 and P3 wait about 100 units, which is a long delay, but both run as soon as P1 finishes. Starvation example under SJF: a long job P1 is waiting while a stream of short jobs keeps arriving, and each time the scheduler picks the shortest job, so P1 can be passed over indefinitely. In Priority scheduling the same happens to a low-priority job while higher-priority jobs keep arriving.
title: What is the difference between the convoy effect and starvation in an example?
page: What is the difference between the convoy effect and starvation in an example?

text: Not in standard FCFS. Processes are served strictly in arrival order, so a waiting process has only finitely many processes ahead of it, and, assuming each of them eventually finishes or blocks, it reaches the head of the queue and gets the CPU. A process can wait a long time behind a long job, but that is the convoy effect: a long, finite delay, not indefinite postponement. Starvation would need an exceptional case, for example a process ahead that never terminates, which is outside the usual assumptions.
title: Can starvation occur in FCFS?
page: Can starvation occur in FCFS?

text: Yes. SJF always selects the ready process with the shortest CPU burst. If shorter jobs keep arriving while a long job is waiting, there is always a shorter job to pick, so the long job can be passed over again and again and may never get the CPU. This is starvation (indefinite blocking). SRTF makes it more likely, because a running long job can also be preempted by each shorter arrival. Whether starvation actually happens depends on the workload: if short jobs stop arriving, the long job eventually runs. Aging is the usual remedy.
title: Can starvation occur in SJF?
page: Can starvation occur in SJF?

text: Priority scheduling always gives the CPU to the ready process with the highest priority. A low-priority process can be bypassed repeatedly if higher-priority processes keep arriving or stay ready, so it may wait indefinitely. This can happen in both preemptive and non-preemptive Priority scheduling, depending on the workload. The usual mitigation is aging: the priority of a process is raised gradually the longer it waits, so eventually even a low-priority process becomes the highest-priority one and gets the CPU.
title: Why can starvation occur in Priority scheduling?
page: Why can starvation occur in Priority scheduling?

text: No. Round Robin does not choose processes by length. It serves the ready queue in cyclic order and gives each process at most one time quantum per turn, then moves it to the back of the queue. A short process whose burst fits within one quantum finishes in its first turn, and so finishes after fewer turns than a long process, but it is not selected first because it is short: it still waits its place in the queue. SJF, not Round Robin, is the algorithm that deliberately picks the shortest job first.
title: Does Round Robin prioritize short processes?
page: Does Round Robin prioritize short processes?

text: Under standard assumptions Round Robin avoids starvation, because every ready process receives a finite quantum in cyclic order and so gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units; it does this by rotating fairly, not by favouring short jobs. SJF does not prevent starvation; it can starve long jobs when shorter jobs keep arriving. SJF does reduce the convoy effect, because short jobs are not stuck behind long ones.
title: Does Round Robin or SJF prevent starvation?
page: Does Round Robin or SJF prevent starvation?

text: SJF and SRTF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Priority scheduling, preemptive or non-preemptive, can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving; aging mitigates this. Under standard assumptions FCFS and Round Robin do not starve a process: FCFS because each process eventually reaches the head of the queue, Round Robin because each ready process gets a turn within (n − 1) × q time units. FCFS can still show the convoy effect, which is a long delay and not starvation.

text: CPU Scheduling — Course Notes (Unit: CPU Scheduling). Compiled for the OS CPU Scheduling Tutor. Conventions follow the prescribed textbook (Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts): a lower priority number means a higher priority, and ties are broken by arrival time and then by process number. Basic concepts. CPU scheduling is the job of the short-term scheduler: whenever the CPU becomes idle it selects one process from the ready queue and the dispatcher gives that process control of the CPU. Process execution alternates between CPU bursts and I/O bursts, which is why scheduling is needed at all. Scheduling decisions happen when a process switches from running to waiting, from running to ready (an interrupt or a timer expiry), from waiting to ready, or when it terminates. If scheduling only happens on the first and last of these, the scheme is non-preemptive (cooperative); otherwise it is preemptive. Dispatcher and dispatch latency. The dispatcher switches context, switches to user mode and jumps to the right location in the user program. The time the dispatcher takes to stop one process and start another is the dispatch latency. Every context switch is pure overhead: no useful user work is done while registers and the process control block are being saved and restored.

text: location in the user program. The time the dispatcher takes to stop one process and start another is the dispatch latency. Every context switch is pure overhead: no useful user work is done while registers and the process control block are being saved and restored. Scheduling criteria. CPU utilisation and throughput should be maximised. Turnaround time, waiting time and response time should be minimised. Turnaround time is the interval from arrival (submission) to completion: turnaround = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time is the total time a process spends in the ready queue: waiting = turnaround − burst time. Response time is the time from arrival until the process first gets the CPU: response = first start time − arrival time. For non-preemptive algorithms response time equals waiting time, because a process runs to completion once it starts. How to solve a scheduling numerical. Step 1: list every process with its arrival time, burst time and priority. Step 2: simulate the algorithm on a time line, deciding at every scheduling point which ready process runs. Step 3: draw the Gantt chart, including idle gaps when no process has arrived. Step 4: read each completion time off the Gantt chart. Step 5: compute turnaround = completion − arrival, then waiting = turnaround − burst. Step 6: average each column. Most lost marks come from a wrong tie-break, from forgetting an idle gap, or from inserting a newly arrived process into the Round Robin queue in the wrong order.

text: FCFS is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm: the process that requests the CPU first is allocated the CPU first. It is implemented with a FIFO queue. When a process enters the ready queue its PCB is linked onto the tail of the queue; when the CPU is free it is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive: once a process has the CPU it keeps it until it terminates or requests I/O. FCFS worked example. Processes P1, P2 and P3 arrive at time 0 in that order with burst times 24, 3 and 3. The Gantt chart is P1 from 0 to 24, P2 from 24 to 27, P3 from 27 to 30. Waiting times are P1 = 0, P2 = 24, P3 = 27, so the average waiting time is (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 17.00. If the same processes arrive in the order P2, P3, P1 the waiting times become 6, 0 and 3, and the average drops to 3.00. The average waiting time under FCFS is therefore generally not minimal and varies a lot with the order of arrival. Convoy effect. Under FCFS all the short processes wait for one long process to get off the CPU, like cars stuck behind a slow truck. With one CPU-bound process and many I/O-bound processes, the I/O-bound processes finish their I/O and sit in the ready queue while the I/O devices go idle, then they all run quickly and go back to I/O while the CPU sits idle. The result is lower CPU and device utilisation. FCFS is particularly troublesome for time-sharing systems, where each user should get a share of the CPU at regular intervals.
title: First Come First Served (FCFS)
page: First Come First Served (FCFS)

text: SJF associates with each process the length of its next CPU burst and gives the CPU to the process with the smallest next burst. If two processes have the same burst length, FCFS order breaks the tie. SJF is provably optimal: it gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes, because moving a short process before a long one decreases the short process's waiting time more than it increases the long one's. SJF worked example. P1 = 6, P2 = 8, P3 = 7, P4 = 3, all arriving at time 0. SJF runs P4 (0–3), P1 (3–9), P3 (9–16), P2 (16–24). Waiting times are P1 = 3, P2 = 16, P3 = 9, P4 = 0, so the average waiting time is (3 + 16 + 9 + 0) / 4 = 7.00. FCFS on the same processes would give an average of 10.25. Predicting the next CPU burst. The real difficulty with SJF is knowing the length of the next CPU request. The usual approach is to predict it as an exponential average of previous bursts: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n), where t(n) is the length of the most recent burst, τ(n) is the past prediction and 0 ≤ α ≤ 1, commonly α = 1/2. With α = 0 recent history has no effect; with α = 1 only the last burst counts. Preemptive SJF is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). When a new process arrives with a next CPU burst shorter than what is left of the currently executing process, SRTF preempts the running process. Non-preemptive SJF lets the running process finish its burst.
title: Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)
page: Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)

text: burst counts. Preemptive SJF is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). When a new process arrives with a next CPU burst shorter than what is left of the currently executing process, SRTF preempts the running process. Non-preemptive SJF lets the running process finish its burst. SRTF worked example. P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8, P2 at 1 with burst 4, P3 at 2 with burst 9, P4 at 3 with burst 5. P1 starts at 0. At time 1 P2 arrives with burst 4, which is less than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is preempted. The Gantt chart is P1 (0–1), P2 (1–5), P4 (5–10), P1 (10–17), P3 (17–26). Waiting times: P1 = (10 − 1) = 9, P2 = 0, P3 = 15, P4 = 2. The average waiting time is (9 + 0 + 15 + 2) / 4 = 26 / 4 = 6.50. Non-preemptive SJF on the same data gives 7.75. Starvation under SJF. A long process can wait indefinitely if short processes keep arriving, because there is always a shorter job to pick; this is starvation (indefinite blocking). SRTF makes it worse because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly.
title: Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)
page: Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)

text: A priority is associated with each process and the CPU is allocated to the process with the highest priority. Equal-priority processes are scheduled in FCFS order. In this course a lower number means higher priority, so priority 1 runs before priority 3. SJF is a special case of priority scheduling where the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst. Priority scheduling can be preemptive (a newly arrived higher-priority process takes the CPU immediately) or non-preemptive (the new process is put at the head of the ready queue). Priority worked example. Five processes arrive at time 0: P1 burst 10 priority 3, P2 burst 1 priority 1, P3 burst 2 priority 4, P4 burst 1 priority 5, P5 burst 5 priority 2. The Gantt chart is P2 (0–1), P5 (1–6), P1 (6–16), P3 (16–18), P4 (18–19). Waiting times are P1 = 6, P2 = 0, P3 = 16, P4 = 18, P5 = 1, so the average waiting time is 41 / 5 = 8.20. Starvation and aging. The major problem with priority scheduling is indefinite blocking, or starvation: a low-priority process can be left waiting forever while higher-priority processes keep arriving. The solution is aging: gradually increase the priority of processes that wait in the system for a long time, for example by improving the priority by 1 every 15 minutes, so that eventually even the lowest-priority process reaches the highest priority and runs.
title: Priority Scheduling
page: Priority Scheduling

text: Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.
title: Round Robin (RR)
page: Round Robin (RR)

text: finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67. Choosing the time quantum. Performance of RR depends heavily on the quantum. If the quantum is extremely large, RR becomes the same as FCFS. If it is extremely small, the system spends most of its time context switching, and each process appears to have its own processor running at 1/n speed (processor sharing). The quantum should be large compared with the context-switch time; a rule of thumb is that about 80 percent of CPU bursts should be shorter than the time quantum. RR typically gives higher average turnaround than SJF but better response time. RR and starvation. Round Robin does not cause starvation. Every process in the ready queue gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, where n is the number of processes and q is the quantum, so no process waits forever. The cost of this fairness is more context switches and therefore more overhead than FCFS or SJF. Context-switch overhead in RR. Because RR preempts a process every quantum, it performs many more context switches than FCFS or SJF. With a quantum of 1 and a process of burst 10 there are 9 context switches for that one process; with a quantum of 12 there are none. Each switch saves and restores the CPU state in the PCB and may flush caches and the TLB, so a very small quantum wastes a large fraction of CPU time.

page: Round Robin (RR)

text: FCFS: non-preemptive, simple, no starvation, suffers from the convoy effect, poor average waiting time. SJF: non-preemptive, optimal average waiting time, needs burst prediction, long jobs can starve. SRTF: preemptive SJF, even lower average waiting time, more context switches, long jobs can starve. Priority: preemptive or non-preemptive, flexible, low-priority starvation fixed by aging. Round Robin: preemptive, fair, good response time, no starvation, performance depends on the quantum, higher context-switch overhead. Multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue. A multilevel queue partitions the ready queue into separate queues, for example foreground (interactive, RR) and background (batch, FCFS), each with its own algorithm and with scheduling between the queues. A multilevel feedback queue lets processes move between queues: a process that uses too much CPU time is moved to a lower-priority queue, and a process that waits too long in a lower queue is moved up, which is a form of aging that prevents starvation.

text: A process is a program in execution: the program's code together with its current activity, which includes the program counter, the registers, the stack and the data. A program is a passive file on disk; a process is the active entity that the operating system creates, schedules and eventually terminates. The operating system keeps each process's information in a process control block (PCB). In a CPU scheduling problem a process is described by an arrival time, a CPU burst time and, for priority scheduling, a priority.
title: What is a process?
page: What is a process?

text: A process moves between five states. New: the process is being created. Ready: it is in memory and waiting only for the CPU. Running: its instructions are being executed on the CPU. Waiting (also called blocked): it is waiting for an event such as I/O completion. Terminated: it has finished execution. The transitions are: new to ready when the process is admitted; ready to running when the dispatcher gives it the CPU; running to ready when it is preempted (a timer interrupt or a higher-priority arrival); running to waiting when it requests I/O or waits for an event; waiting to ready when the I/O or event completes; running to terminated when it exits. CPU scheduling decides which ready process moves to running.
title: What are the states of a process?
page: What are the states of a process?

text: The ready queue holds the processes that are in memory, ready to run and waiting only for the CPU; the CPU scheduler selects the next process from it. A waiting queue (also called a device queue or I/O queue, usually one per device) holds the processes that are blocked waiting for an I/O device or an event. A process leaves the ready queue when it is dispatched. If it then requests I/O it joins a waiting queue, and when the I/O completes it moves back to the ready queue. Only processes in the ready queue compete for the CPU.

text: The cost of a simulation depends on how it is implemented, and is different from the cost of the scheduling algorithm itself. For n processes, sorting by arrival time costs O(n log n). After that, a FCFS simulation needs a single pass over the sorted processes, so the whole simulation is O(n log n), dominated by the sort, and O(n) if the input is already sorted. Non-preemptive SJF and Priority simulations that scan all ready processes at every decision cost O(n2); using a min-heap for the ready queue reduces this to O(n log n). A preemptive simulation that advances one time unit at a time costs O(T × n) for a total running time T if it scans the ready processes at every step, or O(n log n) if it is event-driven with a heap and only decides at arrivals and completions. A Round Robin simulation does constant work per time slice, so it costs O(number of slices), which is about the sum of ceil(burst / quantum) over all processes.
title: What is the time complexity of simulating a scheduling algorithm?
page: What is the time complexity of simulating a scheduling algorithm?

text: The cost of choosing the next process is a property of the data structure the scheduler uses. FCFS and Round Robin use a FIFO queue, so enqueue and dequeue take O(1). SJF, SRTF and Priority scheduling need the minimum burst, remaining time or priority number, which takes O(n) with an unsorted list or a linear scan, and O(log n) per decision with a min-heap (priority queue). The theoretical comparison of algorithms by waiting time is separate from this implementation cost.

text: The ready queue holds at most one entry (a PCB reference) per process, so its space is O(n) for n processes, whether it is a FIFO queue, a sorted list or a heap. A simulation also stores the Gantt chart, which has one entry per execution segment: at most n for a non-preemptive algorithm, and more for preemptive algorithms and Round Robin.

text: SJF gives the minimum average waiting time only if the scheduler knows the length of each process's next CPU burst, and the operating system does not know it in advance. The burst can only be estimated from the past, commonly by exponential averaging: the prediction for the next burst is tau(n+1) = alpha × t(n) + (1 − alpha) × tau(n), where t(n) is the length of the last actual burst, tau(n) is the previous prediction and alpha is between 0 and 1. A wrong prediction removes the optimality guarantee. SJF can also starve long jobs. For these reasons SJF is mostly used as a benchmark or in batch settings where run times are known, and real schedulers use approximations such as the multilevel feedback queue.
title: Why is SJF not practical in real systems even though it is optimal?
page: Why is SJF not practical in real systems even though it is optimal?

text: Context-switch overhead is the time the system spends saving one process's state and loading another's, during which no user process makes progress. Scheduling overhead is the larger cost of running the scheduler itself: examining the ready queue, updating data structures such as a heap, and calling the dispatcher. Both grow when an algorithm preempts often; Round Robin with a very small quantum has high context-switch overhead, while FCFS has the lowest. Textbook numerical problems usually ignore both and treat a context switch as taking zero time.
title: What is the difference between scheduling overhead and context-switch overhead?
page: What is the difference between scheduling overhead and context-switch overhead?

text: Textbook results such as "SJF minimises the average waiting time" assume a single CPU, burst times known exactly, a fixed set of processes and zero context-switch cost. A real system has unknown and changing bursts, I/O, many processes arriving unpredictably, context-switch and cache costs, and goals beyond average waiting time such as response time and fairness. As a result the algorithm that is best in theory on one metric is often not the one used in practice; real operating systems combine ideas, for example a priority-based multilevel feedback queue with Round Robin inside each level.

text: Non-preemptive scheduling lets a process keep the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks; preemptive scheduling lets the operating system take the CPU away mid-burst (on a timer interrupt or a more urgent arrival), which improves response time at the cost of more context switches. Who controls the CPU: Non-preemptive - The running process keeps it until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; Preemptive - The operating system can take it away before the burst is finished. When the scheduler runs: Non-preemptive - Only when the running process finishes or blocks; Preemptive - Also on a timer interrupt and when a more urgent process arrives. Examples: Non-preemptive - FCFS, SJF, Priority (non-preemptive version); Preemptive - Round Robin, SRTF, Priority (preemptive version). Response time: Non-preemptive - Can be poor: one long process makes everyone else wait; Preemptive - Better: short or urgent processes get the CPU sooner. Context-switch overhead: Non-preemptive - Low: a switch only happens when a process ends or blocks; Preemptive - Higher: every preemption is a context switch. Starvation: Non-preemptive - FCFS cannot starve a process; SJF and Priority can starve long or low-priority ones; Preemptive - Round Robin cannot starve a process; SRTF and preemptive Priority can. Shared data: Non-preemptive - Simpler: a process is not interrupted in the middle of updating shared data; Preemptive - Needs care: a process can be interrupted while updating shared data, so synchronisation is required. Best suited to: Non-preemptive - Batch systems where low overhead matters; Preemptive - Interactive, time-sharing and real-time systems. Priority scheduling can be either: it is non-preemptive if a higher-priority arrival must wait, preemptive if it takes the CPU at once.

Needs burst times?: FCFS - No; SJF - Yes (or a prediction); SRTF - Yes (or a prediction); Priority - No (needs priorities); Round Robin - No (needs a quantum). Overhead: FCFS - Lowest; SJF - Low; SRTF - Higher; Priority - Low (preemptive: higher); Round Robin - Highest. Best for: FCFS - Simple batch; SJF - Batch with known run times; SRTF - Known bursts, lowest waiting time; Priority - Jobs of differing importance; Round Robin - Interactive time-sharing. text: Turnaround time is the whole stay from arrival to completion, waiting time is the part of it spent in the ready queue, and response time is only the wait until the first time on the CPU. In non-preemptive algorithms: Waiting time - Equals the response time; Turnaround time - Waiting time + burst time; Response time - Equals the waiting time. text: The long-term scheduler decides which jobs enter memory, the medium-term scheduler swaps processes out and back in, and the short-term (CPU) scheduler picks the next ready process to run, very often. Role: Long-term (job) - Admits jobs from the job pool into memory; Medium-term - Swaps processes out of and back into memory; Short-term (CPU) - Chooses which ready process gets the CPU next. How often it runs: Long-term (job) - Rarely (seconds to minutes); Medium-term - Occasionally; Short-term (CPU) - Very often (every few milliseconds). What it controls: Long-term (job) - The degree of multiprogramming; Medium-term - The degree of multiprogramming, by swapping to relieve memory; Short-term (CPU) - Which process runs on the CPU. Speed needed: Long-term (job) - Can be slow; Medium-term - Moderate; Short-term (CPU) - Must be very fast. Algorithms: Long-term (job) - Not the usual exam algorithms; Medium-term - Swapping policy; Short-term (CPU) - FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Priority, Round Robin. FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are all short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

page: What is the difference between the long-term, medium-term and short-term scheduler?

text: A CPU-bound process computes for long stretches with few I/O waits, while an I/O-bound process uses the CPU in short bursts between frequent I/O waits. Where it spends its time: CPU-bound - Computing on the CPU; I/O-bound - Waiting for input or output. CPU bursts: CPU-bound - Few and long; I/O-bound - Many and short. I/O bursts: CPU-bound - Few and short; I/O-bound - Many and long. Effect on the CPU: CPU-bound - Keeps the CPU busy; I/O-bound - Often leaves the CPU idle while it waits. Scheduling advice: CPU-bound - Gets a lower priority or a lower queue; I/O-bound - Should be favoured: it needs the CPU only briefly and keeps devices busy. A good scheduler favours I/O-bound processes slightly, which improves overall utilisation.

text: Scheduling algorithms are compared on five criteria: two to maximise (utilisation, throughput) and three to minimise (turnaround, waiting, response time). Turnaround time: Goal - Minimise; Meaning - Completion time − arrival time. Waiting time: Goal - Minimise; Meaning - Turnaround time − burst time (time in the ready queue). Response time: Goal - Minimise; Meaning - First time on the CPU − arrival time. In exam numericals the comparison is usually on average waiting time and average turnaround time.

text: The Abstraction: The Process In this chapter, we discuss one of the most fundamental abstract ions that the OS provides to users: the process. The definition of a process, informally , is quite simple: it is arunning program [V+65,BH70]. The program itself is a lifeless thing: it just sits there on the disk, a bun ch of instructions (and maybe some static data), waiting to spring into action. It is the operating system that takes these bytes and gets them running, tr ansforming the program into something useful. It turns out that one often wants to run more than one program at once; for example, consider your desktop or laptop where you might lik e to run a web browser, mail program, a game, a music player, and so forth. In fact, a typical system may be seemingly running tens or even hundreds of processes at the same time. Doing so makes the system easy to us e, as one never need be concerned with whether a CPU is available; one simply runs programs. Mechanism: Limited Direct Execution In order to virtualize the CPU, the operating system needs to som ehow share the physical CPU among many jobs running seemingly at the same time. The basic idea is simple: run one process for a little while , then run another one, and so forth. By time sharing the CPU in this manner, virtualization is achieved. There are a few challenges, however, in building such virtual ization machinery . The first is performance: how can we implement virtualization without adding excessive overhead to the system? Obtaining high performance while maintaining control is thus one of the central challenges in building an operating system. The simple reason: it is a procedure call, but hidden inside that procedure call is the famous trap instruction. More spe cifically , when you call open() (for example), you are executing a procedure call into the C library . Therein, whether for open() or any of the other system calls provided, the library uses an agreed-upon calling con vention with the kernel to put the arguments to open() in well-known locations (e.g., on the stack, or in specific registers), puts the system- call number into a well-known location as well (again, onto the stack or a regis ter), and then executes the aforementioned trap instruction. The code in the library after the trap unpacks return values and returns cont rol to the program that issued the system call. Thus, the parts of the C lib rary that make system calls are hand-coded in assembly , as they need to c arefully follow convention in order to process arguments and return values c orrectly , as well as execute the hardware-specific trap instru ction. And now you know why you personally don’t have to write assembly code to trap into an OS; somebody has already written that assembly for you. One of these is the handling of arguments at the system call boundary; the OS must check what the user passes in and ensure that arguments are pr operly specified, or otherwise reject the call. For example, with a write() system call, the user specifies an address of a buffer as a source of the write call. A Cooperative Approach: Wait For System Calls One approach that some systems have taken in the past (for exampl e, early versions of the Macintosh operating system [M11], or the old X erox Alto system [A79]) is known as the cooperative approach. In this style, the OS trusts the processes of the system to behave reasonably . Processes that run for too long are assumed to periodically give up the CPU so that the OS can decide to run some other task. Thus, you might ask, how does a friendly process give up the CPU in this utopian world? Most processes, as it turns out, transfer contr ol of the CPU to the OS quite frequently by making system calls, for example, to open a file and subsequently read it, or to send a message to anot her machine, or to create a new process. Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue In this chapter, we’ll tackle the problem of developing one of the mos t well-known approaches to scheduling, known as the Multi-level Feedback Queue (MLFQ) . The Multi-level Feedback Queue (MLFQ) scheduler was first described by Corbato et al. in 1962 [C+62] in a sys tem known as the Compatible Time-Sharing System (CTSS), and this work, along with later work on Multics, led the ACM to award Corbato its highest honor, the T uring Award. The scheduler has subsequently been refined throughout the years to the implementations you will encou nter in some modern systems. The fundamental problem MLFQ tries to address is two-fold. Firs t, it would like to optimize turnaround time, which, as we saw in the previous note, is done by running shorter jobs first; unfortunately , the OS d oesn’t generally know how long a job will run for, exactly the knowledge tha t algorithms like SJF (or STCF) require. Second, MLFQ would like to mak e a system feel responsive to interactive users (i.e., users si tting and staring at the screen, waiting for a process to finish), and thus minimiz e response time; unfortunately , algorithms like Round Robin reduce response tim e but are terrible for turnaround time. Thus, our problem: given th at we in general do not know anything about a process, how can we build a scheduler to achieve these goals? How can the scheduler learn, as the system runs, the characteristics of the jobs it is running, and thus make better scheduling decisions? THE CRUX : HOW TO SCHEDULE WITHOUT PERFECT KNOWLEDGE ? Such approaches are c ommon in operating systems (and many other places in Computer Scienc e, including hardware branch predictors and caching algorithms ). Such approaches work when jobs have phases of behavior and are thus predictable; of course, one must be careful with such techniques, a s they can easily be wrong and drive a system to make worse decisions than th ey would have with no knowledge at all. 8.1 MLFQ: Basic Rules To build such a scheduler, in this chapter we will describe th e basic algorithms behind a multi-level feedback queue; although the specifics of many implemented MLFQs differ [E95], most approaches are simi lar. In our treatment, the MLFQ has a number of distinct queues, each assigned a different priority level. At any given time, a job that is ready to run is on a single queue. MLFQ uses priorities to decide which job should run at a given time: a job with higher priority (i.e., a job on a higher queue) is chosen to run. Thus, we arrive at the first two basic rules for MLFQ: • Rule 1: If Priority(A) > Priority(B), A runs (B doesn’t). • Rule 2: If Priority(A) = Priority(B), A & B run in RR. 7.10 Summary We have introduced the basic ideas behind scheduling and deve loped two families of approaches. The first runs the shortest job remain ing and thus optimizes turnaround time; the second alternates between all jobs and thus optimizes response time. text: - Arrival Time: The time at which the process arrives in the ready queue. - Completion Time: The time at which the process completes its execution. - Burst Time: Time required by a process for CPU execution. - Turn Around Time: Time Difference between completion time and arrival time. Turn Around Time = Completion Time – Arrival Time - Waiting Time(W.T): Time Difference between turn around time and burst time. Waiting Time = Turn Around Time – Burst Time

text: Different CPU Scheduling algorithms have different structures and the choice of a particular algorithm depends on a variety of factors. - CPU Utilization: The main purpose of any CPU algorithm is to keep the CPU as busy as possible. Theoretically, CPU usage can range from 0 to 100 but in a real-time system, it varies from 40 to 90 percent depending on the system load. - Throughput: The average CPU performance is the number of processes performed and completed during each unit. This is called throughput. The output may vary depending on the length or duration of the processes. - Turn Around Time: For a particular process, the important conditions are how long it takes to perform that process. The time elapsed from the time of process delivery to the time of completion is known as the conversion time. Turnaround time is the amount of time spent waiting for memory access, waiting in line, using CPU and waiting for I/O. - Waiting Time: The Scheduling algorithm does not affect the time required to complete the process once it has started performing. It only affects the waiting time of the process i.e. the time spent in the waiting process in the ready queue. - Response Time: In a interactive system, turn around time is not the best option. The process may produce something early and continue to computing the new results while the previous results are released to the user. Therefore another method is the time taken in the submission of the application process until the first response is issued. This measure is called response time.

text: CPU scheduling is the process of deciding which process will own the CPU to use while another process is suspended. The main function of CPU scheduling is to ensure that whenever the CPU remains idle, the OS has at least selected one of the processes available in the ready-to-use line. Highest Response Ratio Next (HRRN) Scheduling is a part of non-preemptive CPU scheduling.

text: One of the most optimal scheduling algorithms is the Highest Response Ratio Next (HRNN). This algorithm is a non-preemptive algorithm in which, HRRN scheduling is done based on an extra parameter, which is called Response Ratio. Given N processes with their Arrival times and Burst times, the task is to find the average waiting time and an average turnaround time using the HRRN scheduling algorithm. The name itself states that we need to find the response ratio of all available processes and select the one with the highest Response Ratio. It is designed to improve upon simpler algorithms like First-Come-First-Serve (FCFS) and Shortest Job Next (SJN) by balancing both the waiting time and the burst time of processes. A process once selected will run till completion. below is the formula to calculate the Response Ratio. Response Ratio = (W + S)/S W : Waiting time of the process so far S : Burst time of the process. In HRRN, the process with the highest response ratio is selected for execution next. This approach gives priority to processes that have been waiting longer, but also considers the burst time, ensuring a fair balance between long-waiting and quick-execution processes.

Even processes that need more CPU time will eventually get executed. - Simple to Implement: The algorithm is easy to understand and implement since it only requires calculating the response ratio and selecting the process with the highest ratio. - Dynamic Prioritization: The HRRN algorithm dynamically adjusts priorities meaning that processes which have been waiting longer (but are not necessarily the shortest jobs) will eventually be given higher priority.

text: Priority scheduling is one of the most common scheduling algorithms used by the operating system to schedule processes based on their priority. text: Round Robin Scheduling is a method used by operating systems to manage the execution time of multiple processes that are competing for CPU attention. It is called "round robin" because the system rotates through all the processes, allocating each of them a fixed time slice or "quantum", regardless of their priority. The primary goal of this scheduling method is to ensure that all processes are given an equal opportunity to execute, promoting fairness among tasks. - Process Arrival: Processes enter the system and are placed in a queue. - Time Allocation: Each process is given a certain amount of CPU time, called a quantum. - Execution: The process uses the CPU for the allocated time. - Rotation: If the process completes within the time, it leaves the system. If not, it goes back to the end of the queue. - Repeat: The CPU continues to cycle through the queue until all processes are completed.

text: Shortest Job First (SJF) or Shortest Job Next (SJN) is a scheduling process that selects the waiting process with the smallest execution time to execute next. text: The Shortest Job First (SJF) Scheduling algorithm selects the process with the smallest burst time for execution. But in some cases, the exact burst time of a process may not be known in advance. In such scenarios, an estimation formula is used to predict the next burst time based on the previous burst times. Estimation Formula T_{n+1} = \alpha \cdot t_n + (1 - \alpha) \cdot T_n Where: - T n+1 ​: Predicted burst time for the next process. - T n : Previously predicted burst time. - t n : Actual burst time of the previous process. - α: Smoothing factor (0 ≤ α ≤ 1).

text: The pre-emptive version of Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). In SRTF, the process with the least time left to finish is selected to run. The running process continues until it finishes or a new process with a shorter remaining time arrives, ensuring the fastest finishing process always gets priority.

text: Context switch. In computing, a context switch is the process of storing the state of a process or thread, so that it can be restored and resume execution at a later point, and then restoring a different, previously saved, state. This allows multiple processes to share a single central processing unit (CPU) and is an essential feature of a multiprogramming or multitasking operating system. In a traditional CPU, each process – a program in execution – uses the various CPU registers to store data and hold the current state of the running process. However, in a multitasking operating system, the operating system switches between processes or threads to allow the execution of multiple processes simultaneously. For every switch, the operating system must save the state of the currently running process, followed by loading the next process state, which will run on the CPU. This sequence of operations that stores the state of the running process and loads the following running process is called a context switch. The precise meaning of the phrase "context switch" varies. In a multitasking context, it refers to the process of storing the system state for one task, so that task can be paused and another task resumed. A context switch can also occur as the result of an interrupt, such as when a task needs to access disk storage, freeing up CPU time for other tasks. Some operating systems also require a context switch to move between user mode and kernel mode tasks. The process of context switching can have a negative impact on system performance.

Context switches are usually computationally intensive, and much of the design of operating systems is to optimize the use of context switches. Switching from one process to another requires a certain amount of time for doing the administration – saving and loading registers and memory maps, updating various tables and lists, etc. What is actually involved in a context switch depends on the architectures, operating systems, and the number of resources shared (threads that belong to the same process share many resources compared to unrelated non-cooperating processes). For example, in the Linux kernel, context switching involves loading the corresponding process control block (PCB) stored in the PCB table in the kernel stack to retrieve information about the state of the new process. CPU state information including the registers, stack pointer, and program counter as well as memory management information like segmentation tables and page tables (unless the old process shares the memory with the new) are loaded from the PCB for the new process. To avoid incorrect address translation in the case of the previous and current processes using different memory, the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) must be flushed. This negatively affects performance because every memory reference to the TLB will be a miss because it is empty after most context switches. Furthermore, analogous context switching happens between user threads, notably green threads, and is often very lightweight, saving and restoring minimal context. In extreme cases, such as switching between goroutines in Go, a context switch is equivalent to a coroutine yield, which is only marginally more expensive than a subroutine call.

This means that if the CPU requests data from a disk, for example, it does not need to busy-wait until the read is over; it can issue the request (to the I/O device) and continue with some other task. When the read is over, the CPU can be interrupted (by a hardware in this case, which sends interrupt request to PIC) and presented with the read. For interrupts, a program called an interrupt handler is installed, and it is the interrupt handler that handles the interrupt from the disk. When an interrupt occurs, the hardware automatically switches a part of the context (at least enough to allow the handler to return to the interrupted code). The handler may save additional context, depending on details of the particular hardware and software designs. Often only a minimal part of the context is changed in order to minimize the amount of time spent handling the interrupt. The kernel does not spawn or schedule a special process to handle interrupts, but instead the handler executes in the (often partial) context established at the beginning of interrupt handling. Once interrupt servicing is complete, the context in effect before the interrupt occurred is restored so that the interrupted process can resume execution in its proper state.

User and kernel mode switching. When the system transitions between user mode and kernel mode, a context switch is not necessary; a mode transition is not by itself a context switch. However, depending on the operating system, a context switch may also take place at this time. Steps. The state of the currently executing process must be saved so it can be restored when rescheduled for execution. The process state includes all the registers that the process may be using, especially the program counter, plus any other operating system specific data that may be necessary. This is usually stored in a data structure called a process control block (PCB) or switchframe. The PCB might be stored on a per-process stack in kernel memory (as opposed to the user-mode call stack), or there may be some specific operating system-defined data structure for this information. A handle to the PCB is added to a queue of processes that are ready to run, often called the ready queue. Since the operating system has effectively suspended the execution of one process, it can then switch context by choosing a process from the ready queue and restoring its PCB. In doing so, the program counter from the PCB is loaded, and thus execution can continue in the chosen process. Process and thread priority can influence which process is chosen from the ready queue (i.e., it may be a priority queue). Examples. Then, the hardware switches to kernel mode and jumps into interrupt handler for the operating system to take over. Then the operating system calls the switch() routine to first save the general-purpose user registers of A onto A's kernel stack, then it saves A's current kernel register values into the PCB of A, restores kernel registers from the PCB of process B, and switches context, that is, changes kernel stack pointer to point to the kernel stack of process B. Context switching itself has a cost in performance, due to running the task scheduler, TLB flushes, and indirectly due to sharing the CPU cache between multiple tasks. Switching between threads of a single process can be faster than between two separate processes because threads share the same virtual memory maps, so a TLB flush is not necessary. The time to switch between two separate processes is called the process switching latency. The time to switch between two threads of the same process is called the thread switching latency. The time from when a hardware interrupt is generated to when the interrupt is serviced is called the interrupt latency. Hardware vs. software. Context switching can be performed primarily by software or hardware. Some processors, like the Intel 80386 and its successors, have hardware support for context switches, by making use of a special data segment designated the task state segment (TSS). A task switch can be explicitly triggered with a CALL or JMP instruction targeted at a TSS descriptor in the global descriptor table. It can occur implicitly when an interrupt or exception is triggered if there is a task gate in the interrupt descriptor table (IDT). When a task switch occurs, the CPU can automatically load the new state from the TSS. As with other tasks performed in hardware, one would expect this to be rather fast; however, mainstream operating systems, including Windows and Linux, do not use this feature. This is mainly due to two reasons: Hardware context switching does not save all the registers (only general-purpose registers, not floating-point registers — although the TS bit is automatically turned on in the CR0 control register, resulting in a fault when executing floating-point instructions and giving the OS the opportunity to save and restore the floating-point state as needed). Associated performance issues, e.g., software context switching can be selective and store only those registers that need storing, whereas hardware context switching stores nearly all registers whether they are required or not.
